newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: INTERVIEW-S.Korean Shinhwa sees '97 sales soaring.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-S.Korean Shinhwa sees '97 sales soaring.

text.p: A new telecom device should help push the sales of Shinhwa Co sharply higher to 200 billion won ($227.8 million) in 1997 from 35 billion won in 1996, Shinhwa's chairman said on Thursday.

Chairman Lee Eun-jo said in an interview with Reuters that the annual sales of the new communication and tracking device for use in vehicles and small boats would reach one trillion won by the year 2000.
"Sales can grow even faster than that," Lee said.
He said the potential market for the equipment, called the Tacho Global Positioning System (TGPS), was valued at somewhere between three to six trillion won in South Korea.
South Korea, an untapped market for the system, is expected to have a network for use by TGPS devices by the end of March in the Seoul area and by the end of July elsewhere in the country.
The system, developed over the past three years, allows control centres to track and communicate with vehicles.
Lee said the system was more advanced in comparison with the more widely known GPS, which provides data only about vehicles' operations.
He said the system was expected to help transportation companies save huge costs.
"The system, if fully supplied, would save about 30 percent of transportation costs for land cargo carriers," Lee said.
South Korean companies' land cargo transportation annual costs are now estimated at 13 trillion won, he said.
Lee said Shinhwa would be the sole TGPS provider for some years while potential rivals were catching up with the top-of-the-line technology.
"As far as I know, the TGPS is the most advanced system," Lee said.
Analysts said Shinhwa's heady sales targets were not totally unfounded.
"Shinhwa's development of the system coincides with the need to reduce rising distribution costs," said Choo Hee-yup, an analyst at Dongwon Securities.
Distribution costs currently account for 15.7 percent of the nation's gross domestic product, compared with 10.5 percent in the United States and 8.8 percent in Japan.
The South Korean government set up a task force last year in a desperate effort to bring down the costs, which have emerged as bottlenecks in the economy's growth.
"I believe the use of the TGPS will cut the costs significantly," Lee said.
He said the vacancy rate of running cargo trucks, which now hovered around 35 percent, would be lowered to about five percent with the use of the system.
Lee said his company was expected to benefit from the government's plan to make it mandatory for cargo truck owners to install such systems in their vehicles from 1998.
Analysts said about two million vehicles would use terminals showing information about their operations, such as Shinhwa's system, by the year 2000.
Conversion: $1 = 878 won
